I am seventy-three years old, and I have farmed these fields in Quzhou since I was a young man. My family holds about six mu of good flat land on the North China Plain, and my bones know this soil better than any book. I never went past primary school, but I do not need to — I have watched the seasons turn for sixty years. This year, like every year, I will plant winter wheat after the National Day holiday in early October, and after I cut it in early June, I will put in summer maize the same day without turning the soil, because there is no time to waste and the neighbors have shown me that no-tillage works fine for maize. I use improved wheat seed and hybrid maize seed from the township supply store — the yield is better than the old traditional grains, and everyone in the village buys them now. I will rotary-till before wheat sowing, apply my base fertilizer of compound fertilizer and topdress with urea at green-up, irrigate three or four times for wheat and twice for maize when the dry winds come, and spray for insects, weeds, and once for wheat rust because I have seen what happens if I skip it. I keep some grain for my household and sell the rest to the grain station. It is hard work at my age, but six mu is just enough that I can manage with occasional help from my nephew at harvest.
